sources.title: A Disability Language Style Guide – Franklin County Public Health
sources.excerpt:
# A Disability Language Style Guide
## Consider helpful resources:
### 3. ******Avoid descriptions that imply pity****** .
Disability does not equal suffering! Terms like “afflicted with,” “suffers from” or “victim of” carry the assumption that a person with a disability has a reduced quality of life. Use neutral language when describing a person who has a disability, simply stating the facts.

...

### 6. ******Identity-first language vs. people-first language****** .
In some cases—most notably in the Deaf community and among autistic people—identity-first language is preferred. It’s best to ask the person with the disability how they would like to be described.

### 7. Describing people without disabilities.
“Non-disabled” refers to someone who does not have a disability. According to the [University of Kansas Research & Training Center on Independent Living](http://rtcil.org/products/media/guidelines) , non-disabled is the preferred term when comparing people with and without disabilities.

sources.title: Deaf, deaf – Diversity Style Guide
sources.excerpt:
# Deaf, deaf
Lowercase when referring to a hearing-loss condition or to a deaf person who prefers lowercase. Capitalize for those who identify as members of the Deaf community or when they capitalize Deaf when describing themselves.
Deaf should be used as an adjective, not as a noun; it describes a person with profound or complete hearing loss. Other acceptable phrases include _woman who is deaf_ or _boy who is hard of hearing._

sources.title: Style Guide – The Episcopal Church
sources.excerpt:
# Episcopal Church Writing Style Guide
* [deaf / Deaf](https://www.episcopalchurch.org/styleguide/deaf-deaf/) Lowercase to refer to the audiological status of people with total or significant hearing loss: deaf, hard of hearing. Uppercase when referring to the culture and community of deaf people: Deaf education, the cultural Deaf community.
See also disabilities, Disability Language Style Guide (National Center on Disability and Journalism)
* [diocese](https://www.episcopalchurch.org/styleguide/diocese/)

must_do.rule: Specify in the casting notes that Reyansh must be played by a deaf actor to ensure authentic, first-hand representation.
Describe Reyansh's profound hearing loss using the term 'deaf' in the script.
Capitalize 'Deaf' in action lines when referring to the Deaf community or culture, and use lowercase 'deaf' when referring to Reyansh's audiological status.
Use the term 'non-disabled' in action lines when it is necessary to contrast other characters with Reyansh.

must_not_do.rule: Do not include any scene or plot point where Reyansh's deafness is cured or medically reversed.
Do not use phrases that imply pity, such as 'suffers from' or 'afflicted with', to describe Reyansh's deafness in the action lines.
Do not describe hearing characters as 'normal' or 'able-bodied' in the script's action lines.
Do not use 'deaf' as a noun (e.g., 'the deaf') in the action lines; always use it as an adjective.
